display_title: Official Review of Submission10289 by Reviewer rc6C

summary.value: The paper introduces a new benchmark, MME-Reasoning, designed to evaluate the logical reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs).It comprises 1,188 questions, which are systematically categorized into three reasoning types: inductive, deductive, abductive. The dataset further includes metadata on difficulty (easy/medium/hard), question types (multiple‐choice, free‐form, rule‐based), and capability tags (e.g., pattern analysis, planning & exploring, spatial/temporal). Experiments evaluate a range of state-of-the-art MLLMs (both open-source and closed) across “chat” vs “thinking” modes, which show the cons and pros of current MLLMs.

strengths.value:
1. Curation and metadata richness: The dataset includes multiple dimensions of annotation (reasoning type, difficulty, capability tag, question type) which allows finer‐grained analysis of model behavior rather than only single accuracy numbers, which is critical for both benchmark itself and evaluated models.

2. Focus on reasoning rather than perception and knowledge: The paper tries to filter out questions that are mostly about image recognition or domain‐knowledge recall and push the focus towards reasoning. This improves the validity of the benchmark as a reasoning test.

3. The writing is clear and easy to follow.

weaknesses.value:
1. Knowledge vs reasoning vs perception boundary: While the authors try to reduce dependence on domain knowledge, the distinction between “reasoning” and “heavy factual knowledge” is somewhat fuzzy. Some tasks may still lean on domain knowledge (e.g., biology diagrams, chemistry processes) which adds potential confounds. Likewise, decoupling reasoning and perception is equally difficult, and I hope to see more evidence of both to prove that the benchmark focuses on reasoning.

2. The novelty may be limited.  I think the motivation of this paper is similar to VisualPuzzles[1], EMMA[2] and RBench-V[3]. I hope the author can elaborate on the differences with these works.

[1]:Song Y, Ou T, Kong Y, et al. VisualPuzzles: Decoupling Multimodal Reasoning Evaluation from Domain Knowledge[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2504.10342, 2025.

[2]. Hao Y, Gu J, Wang H W, et al. Can mllms reason in multimodality? emma: An enhanced multimodal reasoning benchmark. ICML 2025

[3]. Guo M H, Chu X, Yang Q, et al. RBench-V: A primary assessment for visual reasoning models with multi-modal outputs. NeurIPS 2025.

3. Abductive reasoning definition and annotation: The classification into inductive/deductive/abductive is useful but also somewhat subjective. The criteria for categorisation, inter-annotator agreement (if any) and the boundary cases might be less well described in the paper. This could limit replicability or interpretability of reasoning‐type results.

comment.value:
**Q1. Knowledge vs reasoning vs perception boundary: While the authors try to reduce dependence on domain knowledge, the distinction between “reasoning” and “heavy factual knowledge” is somewhat fuzzy. Some tasks may still lean on domain knowledge (e.g., biology diagrams, chemistry processes) which adds potential confounds. Likewise, decoupling reasoning and perception is equally difficult, and I hope to see more evidence of both to prove that the benchmark focuses on reasoning.**

**A1**: Thanks for your insightful feedback. We would like to answer the question from the following perspectives:

1. **To quantitatively validate that MME-Reasoning is primarily focused on reasoning and cannot be solved only based on perception, we conduct human and LLM-based evaluations (Tab. 4 in our paper).** We enlist six PhD-level experts, who independently classified questions from our benchmark. As shown in the table, three separate human expert groups determined that 96.1%, 97.3%, and 95.8% of the questions in MME-Reasoning require reasoning.
LLM-Based Evaluation: We also used GPT-4o for the same classification task, which found that 94.4% of the questions require reasoning. These results, consistently showing that over 95% of the benchmark requires reasoning, provide evidence that MME-Reasoning is indeed a reasoning-centric benchmark, especially when compared to another benchmark like MathVista, which scored significantly lower in the same evaluation.

    | | Human Group 1 | Human Group 2 | Human Group 3 | GPT-4o |
    | - | - | - | -| - |
    | MathVista  | 55.7%  | 65.3%   | 52.2%   | 60.7%  |
    | MME-Reasoning | 96.1%  | 97.3%   | 95.8%         | 94.4%  |

2. **To address the concern about the reliance on domain knowledge, we conduct experiments to quantify the amount of knowledge required (Tab.5 in our paper).** Following VisualPuzzles, we generated "knowledge concept checklists" for questions in our benchmark and compared them to a knowledge-intensive benchmark, MMMU. The results show that questions in MME-Reasoning require an average of only 1.4 knowledge concepts, whereas questions in MMMU require 3.9 knowledge concepts. This demonstrates that MME-Reasoning was intentionally designed to minimize the need for heavy factual knowledge, further isolating the core reasoning abilities we aim to evaluate.

    | Benchmark | Question numbers |
    | - | - |
    | MMMU  | 3.9 |
    | MME-Reasoning | 1.4 |

    Further, we agree with the reviewer's point that the biochemistry questions require some domain knowledge. However, we have constrained this knowledge to the K-12 level. During the question collection process, we also conducted extensive testing to ensure that the large models possess the foundational knowledge required to solve them.

3. Finally, we would like to clarify that MME-Reasoning does not decouple perception and reasoning, but goes beyond only perception.

**Q2. The novelty may be limited. I think the motivation of this paper is similar to VisualPuzzles, EMMA and RBench-V. I hope the author can elaborate on the differences with these works.**

**A1**: Thanks for the valuable comment. We will add the comparison between the mentioned benchmarks and MME-Reasoning in our revision. We would like to address this question in the following aspects:

1. **The main design objective of our benchmark is to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of  MLLMs' reasoning capabilities.** To achieve this goal, we collect questions of more diverse reasoning types and question types. Our work is different from the mentioned works in both motivation and data. Below are comparisons with benchmarks the reviewer has mentioned.
2. **Comparison with EMMA**: The key design principle of EMMA is that questions must be answered based on multi-modal inputs and cannot be directly answered from image captions alone. MME-Reasoning aims to conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the models' reasoning capability. Consequently, EMMA's core motivation is distinct from other benchmarks. **EMMA and MME-Reasoning can evaluate different facets of a model's capabilities.**
3. **Comparison with VisualPuzzles**: The motivation behind VisualPuzzles is to decouple perception from reasoning, a goal that aligns with one of our core design principles. It primarily utilizes puzzles that minimize the need for advanced domain knowledge, instead emphasizing observational and inferential skills. In contrast, to achieve a more comprehensive assessment of a model's reasoning capabilities, our benchmark incorporates a wider diversity of question formats and types and reasoning types, as detailed in the table below.

    |Benchmark|Question Types|Reasoning Types|Image Types|Task Types|
    |-|-|-|-|-|
    |VisualPuzzles|MCQ|Inductive,Deductive|Puzzles|Puzzles|
    |MME-Reasoning|MCQ, Free-form, Rule-based|Inductive, Deductive, Abductive|Math, Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Puzzles, Multi-view image, Temporal sequence, Chess and Cards|Spatial, Temporal, Puzzle, Chess and Cards, Geometry, Algebraic, Statistical, Biology, Chemistry, Physics, and other logic games|
4. **Comparison with Rbench-V**: MME-Reasoning and RBench-V serve complementary roles by evaluating different facets of a model's reasoning abilities. **RBench-V is designed to test whether a model can perform reasoning visually.** As an output-oriented benchmark, its goal is to see if a model can "think in pictures" and produce a multi-modal output that reflects its thought process. On the other hand, **MME-Reasoning provides a comprehensive assessment across all major reasoning paradigms to identify a model's specific strengths and weaknesses**. Besides, we list the task types and reasoning types of the two benchmarks below. It can be seen that to achieve a comprehensive evaluation, MME-Reasoning contains a broader range of question types, reasoning types, and task types.
   
    |Benchmark|Question Types|Reasoning Types|Image Types|Task Types|
    |-|-|-|-|-|
    |RBench-V|MCQ, Free-form|Inductive,Deductive|Math, Physics, Counting, Puzzles, Games|Geometry, Physics, Counting, Puzzle, Games|
    |MME-Reasoning|MCQ, Free-form, Rule-based|Inductive, Deductive, Abductive|Math, Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Puzzles, Multi-view image, Temporal sequence, Chess and Cards|Spatial, Temporal, Puzzle, Chess and Cards, Geometry, Algebraic, Statistical, Biology, Chemistry, Physics, and other logic games|

To reply to your comment, we have supplemented the motivation of EMMA and the comparison with VisualPuzzles and Bench-V in Page 3 and Page 17 in the revised manuscript.

**Q3. Abductive reasoning definition and annotation: The classification into inductive/deductive/abductive is useful but also somewhat subjective. The criteria for categorisation, inter-annotator agreement (if any) and the boundary cases might be less well described in the paper. This could limit the replicability or interpretability of reasoning‐type results**

**A3**: Thanks for the valuable comment. We will clarify the annotation process as follows:

1. Each problem was independently evaluated by at least two annotators. Based on our annotation principle in the appendix, if the first two annotators assigned different reasoning types to the same question, the problem was sent to a third annotator for a final decision. In this way, the final reasoning type of each question is only assigned if at least two out of the three annotators are in agreement. 
2. Based on the annotation file, the initial agreement of the two annotators is 78.6% and the remaining 21.4% questions are annotated again by the third annotator. Notably, we observe that no single problem is assigned to three different reasoning types by three different annotators, which indicates that the disagreements were not extreme.

summary.value: This paper introduces a new comprehensive benchmark called MME-Reasoning, designed to evaluate the logical reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). The authors argue that existing multimodal reasoning benchmarks are insufficient for assessing logical reasoning, mainly because they lack a clear taxonomy and coverage of different reasoning types, inductive, deductive, and abductive, and often conflate perceptual ability or knowledge breadth with reasoning ability.

strengths.value:
1. The benchmark follows clear design principles (comprehensiveness, going beyond perception, minimizing knowledge dependence, and diverse evaluation formats), and the construction pipeline is well described.
2. Data are sourced from textbooks, logic workbooks, online resources, exams, existing benchmarks, and author-designed/synthetic problems, with manual filtering to remove items that primarily rely on perception or complex domain knowledge.
3. A broad set of recent, representative MLLMs (closed/open source, chat/thinking models, and rule-based RL models) are evaluated.
4. The paper is well structured and clearly written.

weaknesses.value:
1. The core goal of MME-Reasoning is to systematically assess MLLMs’ logical reasoning—explicitly covering inductive, deductive, and abductive types—while striving to decouple perception and domain knowledge from reasoning. However, many similar benchmarks already exist, e.g.:
   - Can MLLMs Reason in Multimodality? EMMA: An Enhanced MultiModal Reasoning Benchmark
   - VisuLogic: A Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Reasoning in Multi-modal Large Language Models
   - MM-IQ: Benchmarking Human-Like Abstraction and Reasoning in Multimodal Models
     Their data sources likely also contain abductive items, so this benchmark may not clearly reveal deficiencies of current MLLMs relative to what existing benchmarks already show.
2. Much of the data comes from academic exams (e.g., K-12 math/physics), standardized logic questions (civil service exams), and hand-crafted puzzles, with limited coverage of real-world reasoning scenarios. This weakens the benchmark’s ability to assess “real-world reasoning.”
3. Some data (e.g., Chinese civil-service logic questions) may introduce evaluation bias for MLLMs developed by non-Chinese institutions. Such institutions may not train on similar data, whereas Chinese institutions might, making the benchmark less reliable for unbiased capability assessment.
4. The difficulty levels (easy/medium/hard) are defined mainly by the time human experts need to solve each problem, which introduces subjectivity. It would be better to incorporate more objective metrics or report inter-annotator agreement. The paper defines five core abilities, but how this taxonomy was derived—and whether it is standard or newly proposed—should be further justified for soundness and completeness.
5. Typographical error: “casual chain analysis” → “causal chain analysis.”

**Q1. The core goal of MME-Reasoning is to systematically assess MLLMs’ logical reasoning—explicitly covering inductive, deductive, and abductive types—while striving to decouple perception and domain knowledge from reasoning.** 

**A1**: Thanks for the valuable comment. We will add the comparison between the mentioned benchmarks and MME-Reasoning in our revision. We would like to address this question in the following aspects:

1. **The main design objective of our benchmark is to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of MLLMs' reasoning capabilities.** We recognize that a model's reasoning ability cannot be effectively evaluated (1) if the benchmark fails to decouple the knowledge and reasoning (*e.g.*, the model may give a incorrect answer because lacks of the corresponding domain knowledge); (2) if the question relies solely on perception (*e.g.*, the model can directly give the right answer with only 'seeing'). Therefore, **to achieve our primary goal, we established some guiding principles, including decoupling knowledge from reasoning and moving beyond simple perception.**

2. **Comparison with EMMA**: EMMA is motivated by the goal of creating a **multi-modal** benchmark, with a key focus on ensuring that questions cannot be answered by LLMs using only the image caption. Our benchmark emphasizes a comprehensive evaluation of reasoning. Our "beyond perception" principle, for instance, requires that a model must go beyond simple visual tasks like object recognition to arrive at the correct answer. Consequently, the core motivations of the two benchmarks are distinct, and they are complementary, designed to evaluate different facets of a model's capabilities.

3. **Comparison with VisuLogic and MM-IQ**: We have compared MME-Reasoning and other benchmarks in our appendix. Here, we list the differences between MME-Reasoning and these two benchmarks:

    | Benchmark | Question Types  | Reasoning Types | Image Types | Task Types |
    | - | - | - | - | - |
    | VisuLogic | MCQ | Inductive | Puzzles | Puzzles |
    | MM-IQ | MCQ | Inductive | Puzzles | Puzzles |
    | MME-Reasoning | MCQ, Free-form, Rule-based | Inductive, Deductive, Abductive | Math, Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Puzzles, Multi-view image, Temporal sequence, Chess and Cards | Spatial, Temporal, Puzzle, Chess and Cards, Geometry, Algebraic, Statistical, Biology, Chemistry, Physics, and other logic games |

    **Visulogic and MM-IQ focus on evaluating the model's ability to solve puzzle problems, aiming to assess the model's reasoning ability through this type of problem. In contrast, MME-Reasoning is composed of broader question formats, reasoning types, and task types, aiming to give a more comprehensive evaluation of MLLMs' reasoning capability.** Specifically, **(1) In terms of question format**, VisuLogic and MM-IQ are restricted exclusively to Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQ). Our MME-Reasoning benchmark offers a more comprehensive evaluation by expanding beyond this single format. It includes not only MCQs but also Free-form and Rule-based questions, which require models to generate their own answers and demonstrate a deeper understanding of complex tasks. **(2) Broader reasoning types**, Both VisuLogic and MM-IQ focus solely on inductive reasoning, where a model is expected to infer general rules from specific examples, typically within puzzles. MME-Reasoning provides a more comprehensive assessment of a model's reasoning abilities by evaluating three fundamental types of reasoning: inductive, deductive, and abductive. **(3) More image and task types**, VisuLogic and MM-IQ are mainly composed of Puzzles. In contrast, MME-Reasoning utilizes a vastly more diverse and challenging set of materials. The image types include content from various academic fields such as Math, Biology, Chemistry, and Physics, as well as complex formats like multi-view images, temporal sequences, and game boards (Chess and Cards). Consequently, the task types are equally varied, covering Spatial, Temporal, Algebraic, Statistical, and Geometric reasoning, among other logic-based challenges, making it a more comprehensive benchmark.

4. **Finally, we would like to clarify that MME-Reasoning does not decouple perception and reasoning, but goes beyond only perception.**

To reply to your comment, we have supplemented the motivation of EMMA and the comparison with VisuLogic and MM-IQ in Page 3 and Page 17 in the revised manuscript.

**Q2. Much of the data comes from academic exams (e.g., K-12 math/physics), standardized logic questions (civil service exams), and hand-crafted puzzles, with limited coverage of real-world reasoning scenarios. This weakens the benchmark’s ability to assess “real-world reasoning.**

**A2**: Thank you for your valuable feedback. We would like to address your concerns and clarify our design philosophy with the following points:

1. **Core Motivation: A Comprehensive Evaluation** Our primary motivation is to comprehensively evaluate the reasoning capabilities of existing MLLMs. To achieve this, our work incorporates a more diverse range of reasoning types, evaluation metrics, and question sources than previous benchmarks. We believe that only through a broad and multi-dimensional evaluation framework can we accurately pinpoint the strengths and weaknesses of different models, moving beyond comparisons on singular, narrow tasks.
2. **Incorporating Overlooked Reasoning Types** We have placed a special emphasis on balancing reasoning types, especially abductive reasoning. Our analysis revealed that existing benchmarks predominantly focus on deductive reasoning. However, many real-world tasks, such as a doctor diagnosing an illness from symptoms, heavily rely on abductive reasoning—a type that has been largely overlooked in previous evaluations. **To bridge this gap**, our benchmark is the first to systematically and balancedly incorporate all three core reasoning types: deductive, inductive, and abductive.
3. **Integrating Real-World Data** Regarding the comprehensiveness of our data sources, while our benchmark does include academic and standardized questions to ensure rigor, we have also explicitly incorporated data derived from real-world scenarios (*e.g.*, images of daily life scenes). By including the real-world data, MME-Reasoning is more comprehensive than existing benchmarks, such as those focusing on puzzles, and achieves a more comprehensive evaluation. 


**Q3. Some data (e.g., Chinese civil-service logic questions) may introduce evaluation bias for MLLMs developed by non-Chinese institutions. Such institutions may not train on similar data, whereas Chinese institutions might, making the benchmark less reliable for unbiased capability assessment.**

**A3**: Thanks for the constructive suggestion. We would like to clarify from the following perspective:

1. Puzzle is an important question type to evaluate the reasoning capability of multi-modal reasoning. We surveyed a wide range of data sources and found that Chinese civil service exams contain a suitable category of such questions. These problems primarily test abilities like pattern recognition and reasoning, which are fundamentally independent of any specific language or cultural context. Further, we manually filtered the dataset to exclude any questions that contained Chinese characters or other culturally specific elements. Therefore, the selected problems are pure logic puzzles that should not introduce bias against models unfamiliar with the Chinese language or culture.
2. Besides, puzzles from the Chinese civil service exams are not the only source of puzzle questions in our benchmark. We have also incorporated puzzles from other sources, such as puzzle books, to ensure a diverse and comprehensive evaluation. 
3. There are only 79 puzzle questions from the Chinese civil service exam, accounting for 6.6% of the total number of questions in MME-Reasoning. We calculate the results on this type of question as follows:

    | Models | Results |
    | --- | --- |
    |Gemini2.5-pro |39 / 79 |
    |Seed-1.5-pro | 40 / 79|

    The accuracy revealed no consistent correlation between a model's performance and the geographical region of its development institution. In other words, we did not observe that models from Chinese institutions systematically outperformed others on these questions.

**Q4. The difficulty levels (easy/medium/hard) are defined mainly by the time human experts need to solve each problem, which introduces subjectivity. It would be better to incorporate more objective metrics or report inter-annotator agreement. The paper defines five core abilities, but how this taxonomy was derived—and whether it is standard or newly proposed—should be further justified for soundness and completeness.**

**A4**: Thank you for your insightful comment. 

1. We acknowledge that using human expert time can introduce subjectivity. However, we implemented a rigorous, multi-annotator process to ensure consistency and reliability. Our annotation protocol is as follows:

    - Each problem is independently evaluated by at least two annotators.
    - If the first two annotators assign different difficulty levels, the problem was sent to a third annotator for a final decision.
    - The final difficulty level (easy, medium, or hard) is only assigned if at least two out of the three annotators are in agreement. 

    Based on the annotation file, the initial agreement of the two annotators is 69.1% and the remaining 30.1% questions are annotated again by the third annotator. Notably, we observe that no single problem is rated as easy, medium, or hard by three different annotators, which indicates that the disagreements were not extreme. By using this approach with multiple annotators, we aim to create a more objective and reliable difficulty rating than a single expert's estimate would allow.

2. Our taxonomy is based on both empirical analysis of the results, especially failure cases, and cognitive theory. After collecting the problems, we first analyze the error cases generated by various models and try to find the factors that impact a model's reasoning ability. We reference the "Theory of Multiple Intelligences", which was originally proposed by Professor Howard Gardner of Harvard University in his book "Frames of Mind: The Theory of Multiple Intelligences". We retain the intelligences from this theory that are relevant to large models—specifically, Logical-mathematical, Visual-spatial, Intrapersonal, and Naturalist intelligence. By combining these with our own analysis, we modified them to form our final five capabilities. The correspondence between them is as follows:
   
    |Theory of Multiple Intelligences | Explanation | Our Capability |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Logical-mathematical intelligence | Refers to the ability of computation and reasoning | Calculation & Casual Chain Analysis |
    | Visual-spatial intelligence | Refers to the perception, discrimination, memory, and alteration of the spatial relationship of objects. | Spatial & Temporal |
    | Intrapersonal intelligence | The ability to recognize, perceive, and reflect on oneself. | Planning and Exploration |
    | Naturalist intelligence | Refers to an individual's ability to distinguish the environment | Pattern Analysis |

To reply your comment, we have supplemented the overall data annotation process in Page 23 in the revised manuscript.

summary.value: The paper introduces MME-Reasoning, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates LLMs' logical reasoning capabilities and investigates different models' performance with case studies. The dataset is manually curated, covering all three types of reasoning (i.e., inductive, deductive, and abductive). As findings, the benchmark still poses a significant challenge to existing open and closed source models, signifying room for improvements.

strengths.value:

Unlike standard reasoning benchmarks that evaluate the models on hard, domain-specific knowledge, the proposed benchmark tries to evaluate the logical reasoning capabilities of LLMs on their own. This distinction can eliminate, to some degree, the knowledge bias that different LLMs have and focus on their logical inference capacities. 
2. The paper summarizes a list of insights and findings from evaluating different models, including both open and closed source, on MME-Reasoning. The findings are insightful and shed lights on the current limitations of LLMs, as well as giving insights on what contributes to better reasoning performance. 
3. The paper is effortful both in terms of the manual data curation process, the comprehensiveness of the evaluation, as well as the extensive supplementary study delineating the details about the paper. This clearly shows the amount of effort put into this project.

The table shows that the models lag behind human-experts who are PhD students, I wonder how do the models' performance compares with other groups of people. Do the models already achieve on-par performance or they still lag behind?

comment.value:
**Q1. Since logical inference is an ability common to all human beings, I wonder if it also makes sense to access non-human expert's performance on this benchmark and compare that with that of the models. The table shows that the models lag behind human-experts who are PhD students, I wonder how do the models' performance compares with other groups of people. Do the models already achieve on-par performance or they still lag behind?**

**A1**: Thanks to the reviewer for the valuable comments. We agree with the reviewer that conducting human evaluation across different groups of people is meaningful. To provide a more comprehensive comparison between the reasoning abilities of MLLMs and humans, we further conduct a wider human evaluation. We invite five undergraduate students to complete the mini-set of MME-Reasoning. The results are as follows:

|   | Deductive | Inductive | Abductive | Average |  
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| Human Expert (Paper) | 85.8 | 76.9 | 85.6 | 83.4 |
| Human Expert 1 | 78.5 | 73.5 | 84.1 | 78.6 |
| Human Expert 2 | 90.1 | 77.5 | 86.1 | 84.6 |
| Human Expert 3 | 82.1 | 71.5 | 86.1 | 79.9 |
| Human Expert 4 | 75.5 | 76.8 | 83.8 | 78.7 |
| Human Expert 5 | 80.8 | 75.2 | 85.4 | 80.5 |

The results show that while there is some performance variability among human participants, likely due to their diverse backgrounds, they consistently outperform the current models. This shows that there is still a performance gap between existing SoTA models and humans. Besides, we observed that the performance variability among human participants was more pronounced on deductive and inductive tasks compared to abductive ones. We attribute this to the fact that performance on puzzles and mathematical reasoning is often influenced by a participant's specific academic background and expertise. In contrast, abductive reasoning relies on more universal human abilities, such as the capacity for trial, critical thinking, and reflection. Compared to the models, humans have a much stronger ability to learn from trial and error. This results in a more stable and consistently high level of performance on abductive reasoning tasks across participants, regardless of their individual backgrounds.

This extended evaluation confirms that even when compared to non-expert groups, current models still lag behind human-level performance on these reasoning benchmarks. We have revised the manuscript to add the results and analysis in Sec. B.3.

**Q2. Are there any potential biases in the benchmark collected? It seems that the problems main consists of puzzle solving. What would be some of the reasoning tasks that are not covered by the benchmark?**

**A2**: Thanks to your insightful question. We would like to address this question from the following two perspectives:

1. MME-Reasoning includes a broader range of reasoning types and question types, as shown in the following table and our appendix.
   
    | Benchmark | Question Types | Reasoning Types | Task Types |
    | - | - | - | - | 
    | LogicVista | MCQ | Inductive, Deductive |                 Spatial, Scientific, Puzzles |
    | VisualPuzzles |  MCQ | Inductive | Puzzles |
    | VisuLogic | MCQ | Inductive | Puzzles |
    | MME-Reasoning | MCQ, Free-form, Rule-based | Inductive, Deductive, Abductive | Spatial, Temporal, Puzzle, Chess and Cards, Geometry, Algebraic, Statistical, Biology, Chemistry, Physics, and other logic games |

    Besides, compared to existing benchmarks, MME-Reasoning leverages a much broader range of question types and data sources, thereby minimizing the biases that can arise from a narrow data collection process. Besides, MME-Reasoning incorporates more question types, including MCQ, Free-form, and Rule-based questions. This further allows it to include many reasoning problems that were previously difficult to cover.

2. Despite our best efforts, we also acknowledge that it is not feasible to cover every conceivable reasoning task. There are two primary difficulties in benchmarking some types of real-world reasoning questions. The first is a data collection problem: gathering authentic reasoning tasks and their correct answers is a significant challenge. For example, the process of a judge's judgment is an extremely complex reasoning process that is hard to collect and give the correct answer. The second is an evaluation problem: many of these tasks are inherently difficult to score objectively or programmatically through a standardized protocol. For example, in a real scientific scenario, we cannot evaluate the idea using a standardized protocol.

Dear Area Chair and Reviewers,

We sincerely thank you for your time and the constructive feedback provided. We are particularly encouraged by the reviewers' positive recognition of our work, including:

- Clear Design & Reasoning Focus: Appreciating our clear design principles that successfully decouple reasoning from heavy domain knowledge and perception, thereby improving the benchmark's validity.
- Rich Curation & Granularity: Valuing the diverse data sources and rich metadata annotations (e.g., reasoning types, difficulty levels) that enable fine-grained analysis of model behaviors.
- Comprehensive Evaluation: Recognizing the extensive evaluation across a broad set of representative MLLMs and the valuable insights derived from these experiments.

In response to your suggestions for further improvement, we have conducted additional experiments and analyses to address concerns regarding human evaluation, benchmark comparisons, and data rigor. Here is a summary of the key actions we have taken:

- Extended Human Evaluation: We expanded our human performance baseline. The results confirm that while human performance varies, current SoTA models still consistently lag behind humans, particularly in abductive reasoning tasks that require trial and error.
- Clarified Novelty and Comparisons: We provided detailed comparisons with existing benchmarks (e.g., EMMA, VisualPuzzles, RBench-V). We highlighted MME-Reasoning's unique contribution in offering a comprehensive evaluation across all three reasoning types (Inductive, Deductive, Abductive) and a broader range of question formats beyond simple puzzles.
- Clarifying the validated data quality and rigor:
  - Reasoning Focus: We quantitatively verified (via expert and GPT-4o review) that over 95% of our questions rely on reasoning rather than just perception or heavy domain knowledge.
  - Bias & Annotation: We addressed concerns regarding potential data bias (clarifying the minimal and filtered nature of specific data sources) and detailed our rigorous multi-annotator process to ensure objective difficulty grading and classification.

We have carefully revised our manuscript to incorporate these additional results, analysis, and clarifications. We hope these responses effectively address your concerns.

summary.value:
This paper proposes MME-Reasoning, a benchmark for reasoning in multimodal LLMs that aims to address three main gaps in the current multi-modal reasoning literature: 1) going "beyond perception" to ensure that reasoning is evaluated and not simply visual perception, 2) a comprehensive evaluation that encompasses more diverse questions and explicitly tags and evaluates different reasoning types, as well as 3) minimizing knowledge reliance so that reasoning and not specialized knowledge is evaluated.

This work includes a detailed description of the goals and collection process as well closed and open source evaluations.

**However, there were a few key and shared reviewer concerns surrounding proper comparison to the extant literature as well as clear quantitative/qualitative comparisons demonstrating improvements as an evaluation.**

1. very similar motivation was used for several other multi-modal reasoning benchmarks. These also share similar question types.
2. there is lacking evidence that this work has successfully moved the needle on its stated goals

Beyond this, a key claim in this work is that existing models have not yet saturated this evaluation. However, and related to the concerns above, it seems that performance on this benchmark is already passed 50% (note, random chance is much lower than 50%, as questions include MCQA and free-form). This makes it difficult to see that this evaluation is providing a substantial improvement and strong target.

All-in-all, this is an important direction to improve the literature for this category of evaluations. However, there needs to be more quality evidence to suggest this work has a) achieved its stated goals and b) improves on the extant literature.

As two examples, table 4 and 5 are referenced in response to Reviewer rc6C who has these concerns. However, evaluating that this work is less knowledge-heavy than a specifically knowledge-heavy benchmark is not the most informative. This should be extensively compared with the most direct benchmarks in the literature. For table 4 which evaluates if this is actually reasoning, all that is stated is that 6 phd students and gpt4-o were asked. This is not conclusive that this is a better reasoning evaluation.
